title: React components
summary: A component is a JavaScript function that returns UI.
whenToUse: Use components to split the interface into small named pieces that can be reused and reasoned about independently.
do: Keep each component focused on one clear UI responsibility.
Pass data into reusable components with props.
dont: Do not start component names with lowercase letters.
Do not put unrelated screens or workflows into one large component.

codeSnippets.title: Simple component
codeSnippets.description: A component is just a function that returns JSX.
codeSnippets.explanation: React calls the component function and uses the returned JSX to describe the UI.

codeSnippets.title: Practical reusable component
codeSnippets.description: Pass different props to reuse the same UI shape.
codeSnippets.explanation: The Badge component owns the markup, while the parent decides which label to display.

commonMistake: Starting component names with lowercase letters, which makes React treat them like built-in HTML tags.
interviewAnswer: A React component is a reusable function that describes what should appear on the screen for a piece of UI.

courseReference.notes: The project introduces small UI components that combine into a menu screen.

title: Conditional rendering
summary: Conditional rendering shows different UI depending on current data or state.
whenToUse: Use it for loading messages, empty states, toggled panels, validation messages, and alternative views.
do: Use clear boolean names like isOpen or hasItems.
Use early returns when a branch should replace the whole component output.
Keep complex conditions outside the JSX when readability starts to suffer.
dont: Do not hide complicated business logic inside nested ternaries.
Do not render empty placeholder markup when returning null is clearer.

codeSnippets.title: Choose between two views
codeSnippets.description: Use a ternary when both branches should render something.
codeSnippets.explanation: The ternary expression returns one JSX value when isOnline is true and another when it is false.

codeSnippets.title: Render only when needed
codeSnippets.description: Use logical && for a small optional UI fragment.
codeSnippets.explanation: The message appears only when unreadCount is greater than zero.

commonMistake: Using complex nested ternaries directly in JSX until the render logic becomes hard to read.
interviewQuestion: How can you conditionally render JSX?
interviewAnswer: You can use normal JavaScript logic such as if statements before return, ternaries, logical &&, or early returns.

courseReference.notes: Menu items can display different UI depending on their data.

title: Rendering lists
summary: Use array methods like map to turn data into repeated JSX elements.
whenToUse: Use list rendering whenever the UI repeats the same structure for multiple items.
do: Store repeated content in an array and map it to JSX.
Keep the repeated item markup in a small component when it grows.
Provide a stable key for each rendered item.
dont: Do not manually copy and paste repeated JSX for each item.
Do not mutate the array while rendering it.

codeSnippets.title: Map data to JSX
codeSnippets.description: Render one list item for every object in an array.
codeSnippets.explanation: map creates a JSX element for every todo while keeping the UI connected to data.

commonMistake: Mutating the array while rendering instead of mapping existing data to JSX.
interviewQuestion: How do you render a list in React?
interviewAnswer: Map over an array and return JSX for each item, giving each rendered item a stable key.

courseReference.notes: The packing list UI is a practical place to think about rendering arrays.

title: The key prop
summary: A key gives React a stable identity for items in a rendered list.
whenToUse: Use keys whenever rendering siblings from an array so React can update, insert, and remove the right elements.
do: Use a stable id from your data when possible.
Place the key on the element returned directly from map.
Treat keys as identity, not as visible UI data.
dont: Do not use array indexes as keys for lists that can change order.
Do not generate random keys during render.

codeSnippets.title: Use stable ids as keys
codeSnippets.description: The key belongs on the repeated element returned from map.
codeSnippets.explanation: React uses user.id to match each UserRow between renders.

codeSnippets.title: Avoid fragile keys
codeSnippets.description: Indexes are risky when users can add, remove, or reorder items.
codeSnippets.explanation: A real item id stays attached to the same data even when the array changes.

commonMistake: Using the array index as a key for lists that can be reordered, inserted into, or deleted from.
interviewQuestion: Why does React need keys in lists?
interviewAnswer: Keys help React match list elements between renders so it can preserve the correct DOM and component state.

courseReference.notes: List items need stable identity as the list changes.
